newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: JOBS-East Europe reform creates army of jobless.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-East Europe reform creates army of jobless.

text.p: Wrenching economic reform has thrown out of work millions of East European workers, assured under communism of secure jobs for life -- and worse may be in store for parts of the region slow to change.

With the collapse of communism, captive markets and state subsidies disappeared, inflated military budgets were slashed, and frequently inferior Eastern European products were opened to harsh Western competition. Jobs simply vanished.

"For emerging markets economies, it is often the case that a high level of unemployment is a reflection of the fact that restructuring has taken place," said David Lubin, emerging markets economist at HSBC Midland in London.

For countries furthest down the road of economic transition, such as Hungary and Poland, high rates of unemployment may be set to fall. In Bulgaria, Romania and Russia, which lagged others in reform, the dole queues look certain to lengthen as restructuring gathers pace.

The Czech Republic, where unemployment is just four percent, faces a different problem. Low levels of joblessness are helping drive up wages, eroding competitiveness. Czech leaders have complained that unemployment is not high enough.
"The Czech Republic has low unemployment primarily because there has been very little structural change in the economy in the past five years," said Lubin.
In many countries, including Russia and the Baltic states, official statistics mask higher levels of real unemployment. RUSSIAN WORKERS FACE PAYMENTS CRISIS
In Russia, where official data put unemployment at 9.5 percent in January, companies are mired in a payments crisis. Firms often delay wages for months but few have sacked staff.
The crisis has spawned a huge informal "grey" economy.
"For the past five years unemployment in Russia has been chronically understated and is well over 10 percent," the International Labour Organisation said in a report in January.
ILO expert Guy Standing said real unemployment would be higher if many working age men had not disappeared "through premature death" -- whether through suicide, crime or illness.
Suicide and death "seem disproportionately concentrated among the jobless," he said.
In Poland, unemployment stood at 13.5 percent, or 2.34 million people in January, down from 15.4 percent a year ago.
The government has been trying to tackle the problem by tightening up on eligibility for benefits, retraining and with tax breaks for companies investing in unemployment black spots.
Poland's mid-term economic plan assumes that unemployment should fall to single digits by 2000.

Janusz Witkowski, a deputy head of the Polish Central Statistical Office told Reuters that economic expansion and foreign investment should help cut unemployment to about eight percent by 2002, by which time Poland, along with Hungary and the Czech Republic may be European Union members.

Unemployment in Hungary stood at 10.6 percent in January, according to Labour Ministry figures. However, analysts say the statistics can be misleading as high taxes have contributed to the growth of a "grey" economy.
"It makes sense just to call the worker a family member," a Western adviser to the government said.
Things may improve this year with gross domestic product forecast to grow 2-3 percent after two years of minimal growth and real wage declines of about 10 percent a year.

"The 10.6 percent unemployment is unacceptable but given...that the economy is about to start to grow it may be a good outcome given the larger overview," the western adviser said. CZECH WAGE GAINS OUTPACE GROWTH IN INDUSTRY OUTPUT

The Czech government ascribes low unemployment to previously undeveloped service industries, such as tourism, expanding rapidly while political opponents and some economists say it reflects slow restructuring.
"At present everybody thinks unemployment is too low and this is probably the primary reason why our wages are growing so fast," said Vladimir Kreidl, economist at Patria Finance.
Real wages grew 7.9 percent in 1996 compared with a 6.8 percent growth in industrial production for the year.
Kreidl said the low rate reflected the strength of services but also lack of pressure for change from owners of companies.
January's four percent jobless rate, after 3.5 percent in December, was the highest since Czechoslovakia split in 1993 and Kreidel said "a moderate upward trend" was likely.
"If the crown exchange rate depreciates substantially, we will see much more pressure on banks, companies and from the central bank to change behaviour," he said.
Citibank economist Radek Maly said higher unemployment in Bulgaria and Romania did not indicate these countries had made more progress in reform.
"It is difficult to believe that restructuring here (in the Czech Republic) would be so far behind other East European countries," he said.
In Romania, painful reforms which the new centrist government plans this year to put the economy back on track are expected to push many workers out of a job.
The Labour Ministry said around 90,000 people would lose their jobs under the industrial restructuring programme .

According to the latest statistics, 6.7 percent of the workforce or 702,537 people were claiming unemployment benefit at the end of January. But government officials say unemployment will not exceed 8.0 percent this year, as faster privatisation is expected to absorb some of the jobless.
In Bulgaria, undergoing a severe economic crisis, a caretaker cabinet appointed in early February, has pledged to close loss-making firms and speed up privatisation.

"Bulgaria's unemployment will rise steadily in 1997 due to expected urgent economic stabilisation measures and eventual introduction of a tough fixed exchange rate regime," a National Labour Exchange (NLE) official said.
The number of unemployed rose to 512,992 or 13.4 percent of the workforce in January from 12.5 percent in December, NLE data show.
Slovak unemployment stood at 13.59 percent in January. The dissolution of old collective farms has meant the highest unemployment is in rural areas linked to agricultural industry.
In the Baltic states, analysts say real unemployment may be double the official four percent in Estonia, six percent in Lithuania and seven percent in Latvia.
